Michael Hudson and Radhika Desai start with the question of undemocratic behavior in the EU, namely the impression of Ukraine men into military serviced and the constitutional court confrontation in Poland and in what they and the US midterms vote say about the condition of what passes for democracy. By Radhika Desai. Published at Geopolitical Economist Radhika Desai: Hello and welcome to another Geopolitical Economy Hour, the socialist and anti-imperialist conversation that illuminates the fast changing political economy and geopolitical economy of our times. You’re watching Radhika Desai, Geopolitical Economist, and I’m Radhika Desai. Today’s show is our regular fortnightly with Michael Hudson. Welcome, Michael. Michael Hudson: It’s good to be here. Radhika Desai: Michael, you and I were going to talk about the upcoming midterms. We are recording on the morning of Tuesday, the 3rd of November, when they are taking place across the United States. And we were going to discuss what was involved in them and so on, and we will discuss that. But meanwhile, as we were talking about what we were going to say, we were confronted with another crisis. I mean, the midterms are shaping up to be a bit of a crisis already, given that we have no idea how Donald Trump will respond if and when the results turn out to be what they are widely predicted to be, which is a Democratic sweep. Now, Trump may react in a whole range of different ways, creating a constitutional crisis in the United States. But here is another constitutional crisis which has some sort of parallels with what may happen in the United States. So in Poland, there was a constitutional crisis sparked just last Friday because President Karol Nawrocki refused to appoint five of the eight judges recommended by Prime Minister Donald Tusk to the Constitutional Tribunal. Tusk then tried to force the issue by getting his unappointed judges to claim that the Chief Justice, who had been appointed by the previous conservative right-wing PiS government, had been suspended, and also tried to use the police to prevent the Chief Justice from entering the court. Now, President Nawrocki, who was on his way to Senegal for some kind of summit, turned the plane around, returned to Poland, got into the court building, and there held a press conference accusing the government of forcibly seizing a constitutional institution. And as we speak, both sides remain intransigent. I can see at least three different axes of confrontation here. One is between the liberal EU oriented elite represented by Donald Tusk, the Prime Minister, and on the other hand, the conservative populists of the PiS variety represented by President Karol Nawrocki. That’s the first one. The second one is a confrontation between those who would be happy to participate in Europe’s war on Russia, using Ukraine as a proxy, and those who are not at all sure this is a good idea. And then there are those who favour the EU and those who think that the United States is a better partner. And here it seems that a lot of what’s involved is who Poland is going to buy arms from, whether it’s for its own defence or to take part in the Ukraine war, et cetera. So Michael, what’s your take, and what are the parallels you see with the situation in the United States? And this whole issue of the West essentially going on and on about democracy while it is being visibly hollowed out in the heartlands of the West itself. Michael Hudson: Well, in our discussion before the show, we agreed that the common denominator between Poland and the United States is the question of what is a democracy. And if you look at the whole history of Western civilization, Aristotle already said long ago that what constitutions call democracy are really oligarchies. And the problem for oligarchies for the last maybe twenty-five hundred years is how do you prevent democracy, literally rule by the majority, so that it is controlled by the minority? And there are many ways of doing this. One of the ways was to divide what you could call a parliament into two houses. The Senate meant the elderly in antiquity, and by medieval times in Europe and America, it meant the large landowners, who sat for a much longer term to prevent parliaments from doing anything that’s democratic. But then one of the additional ways of checking democracy is to say, well, in the popular idea, democracy is that everybody gets to vote. Okay, you’ve got to let everybody vote. The key, as the ancient Romans decided, is how do we make their votes not count? And that really is the common denominator between Poland and the United States right now. The way that they’ve decided to make votes not count is to make the actual implementation of any policy that Parliament might pass, that the majority might pass, subject not only to the Senate veto, but to a constitutional court. That’s the problem today. In the United States, this is the most expensive campaign process in history. And the Supreme Court has ruled that, well, we’ve got to do it the way the Romans did. The Romans assigned weighted votes to the wealthiest Roman constituency, much higher than the votes of the agrarian people as a whole. And so when the wealthiest classes voted, their votes, maybe the one to ten percent, outweighed the ninety percent. So that made sure that there wouldn’t really be a democracy there. Well, the same thing happened in the United States. If you read the Federalist Papers, Alexander Hamilton and especially James Madison said, well, democracy is a threat to the wealthy people. They oppose banking. They oppose the large landowners. How do we keep them in check? Well, we’ve got to have a Supreme Court, and we’ve got to have various ways of making sure that their votes don’t count. Well, the Supreme Court has said just that, that voting should reflect the wealth of the classes that pay for the political campaigns of the candidates who are running in the primaries. And as long as you can have private funding, then essentially the politicians are up for sale. It’s what Americans call pay-to-play. And if you’re a politician and you want to run in a primary, or if you win the primary and run as either a Democrat or a Republican against the opponent, you’ve got to find financial backers who are going to pay for the campaign expenses, and especially the media expenses, the television ads, the radio ads, the newspaper ads and all of the campaigning. That’s what’s been happening in the United States, and we’ll get to this election in a minute. This is the most expensive campaign in history, and one of the issues of the campaign is that either the Republicans or the Democrats will say, well, my opponent is funded by AIPAC, and a vote for my opponent being funded by AIPAC is a vote for the war that is pushing up your oil prices, your gas prices, your diesel prices, your fertilizer prices and all that. So you could say that the whole issue is who is funding which candidates. And in Poland, the process you described is particularly tricky because when parliament passes a law proposed by the Prime Minister, the President has to approve it. And as it happens in Poland, the Prime Minister, Tusk, his party is essentially the European Union party. And the Americans say Tusk is representing democracy in trying to appoint his judges, who will rule in his favour and subordinate Polish laws to the EU laws. And the EU laws are controlled by the European Commission in Brussels, by von der Leyen and Kaja Kallas. And America says that the opposing party, the Law and Justice party, is called democratic, but it’s populist and nationalist. The Law and Justice party was formed out of the Solidarity trade union movement, and its backers are on the land and in the small towns that have been left behind by the whole neoliberalization of Polish development. And the United States says, well, populism and nationalism may have the votes, but that’s not democracy. Democracy is whoever we say is pro-American. And look at the leading democracies according to the United States. They are Ukraine, the most corrupt, kleptocratic country in the northern hemisphere, and Israel. Any country that is pro-American is a democracy. And in fact, the United States has created an institution, the National Endowment for Democracy, to fund and stage demonstrations. And obviously Tusk’s party staged a demonstration against the court, trying to support Tusk’s takeover, saying that you cannot have a democracy in Poland that outweighs what the unelected EU bureaucracy in Brussels states. And Brussels states, well, we want Poland to have a stipulated level of immigrants that it has to take, especially from Ukraine. Poland and Ukraine are not very friendly, so you can imagine how the Polish voters feel. And the EU laws want to force all of their members to back the war on Russia being fought largely in Ukraine, and to pay for the militarization, and essentially to bring Poland under the domination of the German, anti-Russian, Christian Democrat neoliberals under Merz. Well, what you’re seeing right now, in addition to Poland’s constitutional crisis, is riots all over Europe. You’ve seen the French riots in the papers. You’ve seen in Albania the riots against Donald Trump’s son-in-law, who’s made a corrupt deal with the Arab Emirates to try to develop seafronts. You’re having riots all over Europe. So what the papers call a constitutional crisis, from Poland to Albania to the United States, is really the culminating fight of the neoliberal globalist oligarchy against democracy. That’s what we’re seeing at the broadest level. Radhika Desai: I agree substantially with what you say, although I wonder if it is a straightforward fight between what you’re calling the EU globalist elite and democracy. Because remember, what’s ranged against the EU elites is not necessarily any kind of progressive or democratic force. It’s a conservative populist party which has its own set of problems. So we’re looking at an extremely complex situation here, in which any kind of serious democracy that genuinely has the interests of the vast majority of the people at heart is kind of lost somewhere in all this mayhem. And this is as true of the United States as it is of Poland. I was also interested to see, by the way, that even the Financial Times, which you’d normally think would have sided one-sidedly with the European Union on this matter because it’s very Atlanticist, very pro-EU and all that, could not find it in itself to do so, because it is painfully aware that the pro-European side, the Donald Tusk side in Poland, is using the same sort of unconstitutional manoeuvres to gain its position as the PiS, according to the Financial Times, has done. So the Financial Times’ case is that the PiS packed the court with its own people. Now the terms of some of those who had originally been appointed by the PiS have expired, so Donald Tusk is now taking the opportunity to appoint these people. But interestingly, the Financial Times can’t really choose between the PiS and Tusk, but it certainly takes the side of the European Union and defends the European Union’s power to intervene in the domestic affairs of its member states by essentially withholding European Union funds when they are seen to step out of line. And by the way, this is also very interesting. The European Union keeps saying that it is withholding funds in order to protect democracy and constitutionalism and what have you. But in reality, what it’s doing is enforcing neoliberalism. Now, I just wanted to clarify that, but let me pick up on some of the really good, substantial points you’ve made. So first of all, you started off with Aristotle. And I think it’s very important for us to remember that until the 20th century, practically no major intellectual, and that includes Aristotle, thought democracy was a good thing. They all thought it was an awful thing, something that must be prevented, because it gave power to those who did not have property and gave them power to act against the interests of property. So I think that at least back then they were very brazenly forthright about what side they stood on. Since the 20th century and the advent of mass politics, it has been very difficult for the elites of most Western societies and beyond to openly voice anti-democratic sentiments. So everybody claims to be democratic, but as you rightly pointed out, while they claim to be democratic, they are constantly looking for ways in which they could ensure that the democratic rights of ordinary people do not count. And this is done in two principal ways, and these are both getting absurd. One of them is, of course, to invoke constitutionalism and liberalism above democracy. So you say that there are constitutional limits to what a majority can do. So the majority, for example, cannot expropriate the wealth of any part of society. This is usually constitutionally forbidden. So there is that sort of limit. The second way in which you do it, which is happening more and more in Europe now, is to invoke some kind of higher principle over democracy. So you say that you stand for the rights of Ukraine, and no matter how unpopular your position is, you are going to stick by it because this is somehow superior to the democratic principle. And this is what you see people like Annalena Baerbock doing when she says, I stand for Ukraine, even though the vast majority of Germans do not wish me to do so, and what a wonderful political leader I am. And last but hardly least, you spend money on elections. You spend money on disinformation, beguiling people, misleading them into voting for that which is not in their own interest and so on. And as you rightly pointed out, I was shocked to discover that this midterm election, Michael, is the most expensive in US history. It is more expensive than the last presidential election of 2024. Just think about how much is invested here. And what’s more, given how brazenly the elite acts these days, we know that people like Elon Musk have given close to half a billion dollars to the Republicans. They have said so openly. They have given half a billion dollars to the Republicans in order to fight the elections. Elon Musk is the richest man in the world, and other almost equally rich people have also been making extremely substantial contributions. Websites like OpenSecrets have clearly shown that the amount of money is not only great, but an enormous amount of it is dark money. It is secret money. So in all of these ways, efforts are made to ensure that the voice of ordinary people is not heard. And maybe I’ll add one final thing. One of the big problems that we face today is that there is no doubt in the minds of ordinary people that what our governments are doing is not in our interest.
